title: Aggregate demand
competency: Define aggregate demand, explain why the AD curve slopes down, and distinguish a change in quantity demanded from a change in aggregate demand.

keywords.def: The total amount all sectors (households, firms, government, foreigners) are ready to spend on an economy's goods and services in a period: AD = C + I + G + (X − M).
Household spending (C), mainly set by disposable income, wealth, income trends and the price level.
Private spending (I) on structures, equipment and inventories, set by output, the cost of capital and expectations.
Government spending on goods and services (G), set directly by government decisions.
Exports minus imports (X − M); negative when imports exceed exports.
A downward-sloping curve showing the real output buyers want at each price level, other things equal.
A higher price level lowers the real value of money holdings, so people buy less real GDP (also called the wealth effect).
A higher price level raises money demand and the interest rate, so investment and interest-sensitive consumption fall.
A higher domestic price level makes home goods dearer than foreign goods, so exports fall and imports rise.
A movement along the same AD curve caused only by a change in the price level.
A shift of the whole AD curve caused by a change in spending at a given price level.
Personal income minus taxes: take-home pay.
A currency appreciates when more foreign currency is needed to buy one unit of it.
A currency depreciates when more of it is needed to buy one unit of a foreign currency.

en.text: Aggregate demand is the total amount households, firms, government and foreigners are ready to spend on an economy's goods and services in a period. It has four components: AD = C + I + G + (X − M). Net exports can be negative when imports exceed exports, and then they lower AD.

am.text: ጠቅላላ ፍላጎት የሁሉም ዘርፎች ጠቅላላ ወጪ ነው፤ AD = C + I + G + (X − M)። ገቢ ንግድ ከወጪ ንግድ ሲበልጥ የተጣራ የውጭ ንግድ አሉታዊ ይሆናል።

screens.title: Who is spending?
screens.ask: In one year, families in Hawassa buy food. A firm in Adama builds a factory. The government builds a road. A buyer in Germany buys Ethiopian coffee. Which spending counts in demand for Ethiopian output?
opts: Only the families and the firm
screens.after: All four count. Spending comes from households, firms, government and foreigners.

screens.title: What is aggregate demand?
paras: Aggregate demand (AD) is total planned spending in an economy.
It is the money all sectors are ready to spend in a given period.
The sectors: households, firms and government (and foreigners).
They spend on goods and services produced in the economy.
AD depends on the price level, monetary policy, fiscal policy and other factors.

screens.title: The four components
paras: AD = C + I + G + (X − M)
table: disposable income, wealth, income trends, price level
level of output, cost of capital, expectations
domestic and foreign incomes, relative prices, exchange rates

screens.title: Worked example: total AD
steps: Imports exceed exports, so net exports subtract from AD.

screens.ask: C = 500, I = 100, G = 150, X = 80, M = 30 (billion Birr). AD = ___ billion Birr
screens.clue: Add C, I and G, then add (X − M).

screens.title: Match each component with what mainly determines it
pairs: incomes, relative prices and exchange rates
screens.why: p.27 lists the main determinant of each component.
screens.clue: Who decides each kind of spending?

screens.text: Which spending is part of investment (I)?
opts: A firm in Adama buys new machines
The government pays for a road
screens.ans: A firm in Adama buys new machines
screens.why: Investment is private spending on structures, equipment and inventories. Teff is C, the road is G, coffee sold abroad is X.
screens.clue: Who is buying, and what?

screens.ask: Ethiopia exports 120 and imports 170 (billion Birr). Net exports = ___ billion Birr
screens.why: X − M = 120 − 170 = −50. Imports exceed exports, so net exports are negative.
screens.clue: Exports minus imports.

screens.why: When imports exceed exports, X − M is negative and lowers AD.
screens.clue: Compare exports and imports.

screens.text: The book also says AD is "total expenditure on consumption and investment". When is that complete?
opts: Only with no government and no foreign trade
Never, because AD leaves out consumption
screens.ans: Only with no government and no foreign trade
screens.why: With government and trade, AD = C + I + G + (X − M). C + I alone fits only a two-sector economy.
screens.clue: Which components are missing?

screens.ask: C = 700, I = 200, X = 150, M = 250 and AD = 1000 (billion Birr). G = ___ billion Birr
screens.clue: Find net exports first, then subtract the known parts from AD.

ideas.name: The AD curve and why it slopes down

en.text: The AD curve shows how much real output buyers want at each price level, other things equal. It slopes down: a lower price level raises the quantity of real GDP demanded. Three effects explain this: the real balance effect (money buys more), the interest rate effect (lower money demand, lower interest rates, more investment) and the international trade effect (home goods cheaper than foreign goods).

am.text: የጠቅላላ ፍላጎት ኩርባ ወደ ታች ያዘነብላል። ምክንያቶቹ፡ የገንዘብ ሀብት ውጤት፣ የወለድ ምጣኔ ውጤት እና የዓለም አቀፍ ንግድ ውጤት ናቸው።

screens.title: Prices fall everywhere
screens.ask: Prices of almost all goods in Ethiopia fall, but the money people hold stays the same. What happens to the total amount of goods people want to buy?
screens.after: Money buys more, so people demand more real output. The price level and real GDP demanded move in opposite directions.

screens.title: The AD curve
paras: The AD curve shows real output buyers want at each price level.
Other factors are held constant (ceteris paribus).
Price level is on the vertical axis; real GDP on the horizontal axis.
The relationship is inverse, so the curve slopes down.
Figure 2.1: the price level falls P₁ → P₀; quantity demanded rises Q₁ → Q₀.
It is the law of demand (Grade 9) for the whole economy.

screens.title: Why it slopes down: three effects
paras: Each effect starts with a rise in the price level.
table: money holdings buy less; people feel poorer
money demand rises; with fixed money supply the interest rate rises; I and C fall
Ethiopian goods dearer than foreign goods; Ethiopians and foreigners buy fewer

screens.title: Interest rate effect: one firm's decision
steps: A firm expects a 6% return on a new machine.
The price level rises → money demand rises → the interest rate rises to 7%.
Consumers also put off buying houses and cars.
So a higher price level reduces real output demanded.

screens.title: Key words
defs: Aggregate demand curve
A downward-sloping curve showing the real output buyers want at each price level, other things equal.
Real balance effect
A higher price level lowers the real value of money holdings, so people buy less real GDP (also called the wealth effect).
Interest rate effect
A higher price level raises money demand and the interest rate, so investment and interest-sensitive consumption fall.
International trade effect
A higher domestic price level makes home goods dearer than foreign goods, so exports fall and imports rise.

screens.text: A rise in the price level makes money holdings buy less, so people buy less. This is the
screens.why: It works through the value of monetary wealth (money holdings).
screens.clue: Which effect is about the money people hold?

screens.title: Match each effect with how it works
pairs: purchasing power of money holdings changes
money demand and interest rates change
home goods become dearer or cheaper than foreign goods
screens.why: The three reasons on p.28–29.
screens.clue: Look for money, interest or foreign goods.

screens.ask: A household holds 10000 Birr. The price index rises from 1.00 to 1.25. Its money is now worth ___ Birr in base-year prices
screens.why: 10000 ÷ 1.25 = 8000 Birr. It is 20% poorer in real terms, so it buys less.
screens.clue: Divide by the new price index.

screens.title: Put the interest rate effect in order
screens.why: With a fixed money supply, more money demand pushes up its price, the interest rate.
screens.clue: The interest rate is the price of using money.

screens.text: A firm expects a 6% return on a project. At which interest rate is the project NOT worth doing?
screens.why: Borrowing at 7% costs more than the 6% return: 6% − 7% = −1%.
screens.clue: Compare return with the cost of borrowing.

screens.text: The price level in Ethiopia FALLS. Which chain is correct?
opts: Money demand falls → interest rate falls → investment rises → real GDP demanded rises
Money demand rises → interest rate rises → investment rises → real GDP demanded rises
Ethiopian goods become dearer → exports fall → real GDP demanded rises
Real value of money falls → people buy more → real GDP demanded rises
screens.ans: Money demand falls → interest rate falls → investment rises → real GDP demanded rises
screens.why: All three effects work in reverse when the price level falls. Only the first chain has every link right.
screens.clue: Check each arrow on its own.

en.text: A change in the price level moves the economy along the AD curve; this is a change in aggregate quantity demanded. Anything else that changes spending at a given price level shifts the whole curve; this is a change in aggregate demand. AD shifts right when C, I, G or net exports rise: higher wealth, expected higher prices or income, lower interest rates, lower income or business taxes, business optimism, more government purchases, higher foreign income or a depreciating Birr. A higher real interest rate shifts AD left.

am.text: የዋጋ ደረጃ ለውጥ በኩርባው ላይ እንቅስቃሴ ነው፤ ሌሎች ለውጦች ኩርባውን ያንቀሳቅሳሉ። የወለድ ምጣኔ ሲጨምር AD ወደ ግራ ይሄዳል፤ ብር ሲዳከም AD ወደ ቀኝ ይሄዳል።

screens.title: Guess: movement or shift?
screens.after: Only a change in the price level moves us along the curve. Anything else shifts the whole curve.

screens.title: Movement or shift?
paras: A change in the price level changes the quantity of real GDP demanded.
That is a movement along the same AD curve (Figure 2.2a, A → B).
A change in aggregate demand is a shift of the whole curve (Figure 2.2b).
Increase: AD₀ → AD₁ (right). Decrease: AD₀ → AD₂ (left).
In a shift, quantity demanded changes even at the same price level.

screens.title: What shifts AD?
paras: At a given price level, if C, I, G or net exports rise, AD shifts right.
If they fall, AD shifts left.
table: wealth ↑; higher future prices or income expected; interest rate ↓; income tax ↓
interest rate ↓; optimism about sales; business tax ↓

screens.title: Careful: the real interest rate
paras: The book lists AD determinants: income, the real interest rate, foreign activity, credit, home activity.
It says a "positive change" in any of them shifts AD right.
That is wrong for the real interest rate.
A HIGHER real interest rate shifts AD LEFT: I and C fall.
A LOWER real interest rate shifts AD right.
The book itself says so on pp.32–33.

screens.title: Exchange rates and net exports
paras: Appreciation: more foreign currency is needed to buy one Birr.
Depreciation: more Birr is needed to buy one unit of foreign currency.
Birr depreciates → imports dearer, Ethiopian goods cheaper abroad → X ↑, M ↓ → AD ↑.
Birr appreciates → X ↓, M ↑ → AD ↓.

screens.title: Worked example: the leather jacket
steps: An Ethiopian leather jacket costs 1500 Birr.
At 1 Birr = 2 Rupee, in India it costs 1500 × 2 = 3000 Rupee.
The Rupee depreciates to 3 Rupee = 1 Birr.
Now it costs 1500 × 3 = 4500 Rupee in India.
The Birr price did not change; the Indian buyer pays 1500 Rupee more.

screens.title: Key words
defs: Change in aggregate quantity demanded
A movement along the same AD curve caused only by a change in the price level.
Change in aggregate demand
A shift of the whole AD curve caused by a change in spending at a given price level.
Disposable income
Personal income minus taxes: take-home pay.
Appreciation
A currency appreciates when more foreign currency is needed to buy one unit of it.
Depreciation
A currency depreciates when more of it is needed to buy one unit of a foreign currency.

screens.text: Which causes a SHIFT of the AD curve, not a movement along it?
opts: The general price index goes up by 5%
screens.why: Lower taxes raise disposable income and consumption at every price level. Price-level changes only move us along the curve.
screens.clue: Is the price level the cause?

screens.title: AD shifts right or left?
items: Firms become pessimistic about future sales
screens.why: Ask which component changes (C, I, G or NX) and whether it rises or falls.
screens.clue: Find the spending component first.

screens.ask: Monthly income is 10000 Birr. The income tax rate rises from 15% to 20%. Disposable income falls by ___ Birr
screens.why: 15%: 10000 − 1500 = 8500. 20%: 10000 − 2000 = 8000. Fall = 500 Birr, so C falls and AD shifts left.
screens.clue: Work out take-home pay at each rate.

screens.ask: A jacket costs 2000 Birr. 1 Birr = 2 Rupee, then the Rupee depreciates to 3 Rupee = 1 Birr. The new price in India is ___ Rupee
screens.clue: Price in Rupee = price in Birr × Rupee per Birr.

screens.text: A rise in the real interest rate shifts the AD curve to the right.
screens.why: A higher real interest rate lowers investment and interest-sensitive consumption, so AD shifts LEFT. The list on p.29 wrongly suggests otherwise.
screens.clue: What happens to borrowing when loans cost more?

screens.text: The exchange rate changes from $1 = 32 Birr to $1 = 25 Birr. What happened?
screens.why: Fewer Birr are needed to buy one dollar, so each Birr is worth more. Net exports and AD would fall.
screens.clue: Count the Birr needed for one dollar.

screens.ask: A bag of Ethiopian coffee costs 640 Birr. The rate moves from $1 = 32 Birr to $1 = 55 Birr. Its dollar price falls from $20 to $___ (2 decimal places)
screens.why: 640 ÷ 32 = $20 before; 640 ÷ 55 ≈ $11.64 after. The Birr depreciated: coffee is cheaper abroad, exports rise, NX and AD rise.
screens.clue: Dollar price = Birr price ÷ Birr per dollar.

test.text: Which is a movement along the AD curve?
test.why: Only a price-level change moves along the curve.

notes.text: p.29: the book says a "positive change" in any AD determinant (including the real interest rate) shifts AD right. A RISE in the real interest rate shifts AD LEFT (as pp.32–33 say). The lesson teaches the corrected fact.
p.28: "aggregate demand rises with a fall in the general price level" should read "aggregate quantity demanded rises" (a movement, not a shift); the lesson uses quantity demanded.
p.26: "AD is the total expenditure on consumption and investment" holds only for a two-sector economy; p.27 gives AD = C + I + G + (X − M).

p.29: "a shift from AD₁ to AD₂" clashes with Figure 2.2b (AD₀ original, AD₁ increase, AD₂ decrease). p.31: the box "C ↑ ⇒ G ↑ ⇒ NE ↑ ⇒ AD ↑" drops investment and reads as a causal chain; meaning: C, I, G or NE ↑ ⇒ AD ↑.
p.34: the change "$1 = 32 Birr to $32 = 1 Birr" is unrealistic and the next sentence is circular. The lesson uses $1 = 32 → 25 Birr (appreciation) and 32 → 55 Birr (depreciation), marked added.
Worked Birr numbers (AD sums, 10000-Birr household, income tax, coffee) are added for practice. Hook place names are added.
